introduction-the-nervous-system-of-aws.core: EventBridge is a serverless event bus: producers publish JSON events describing what happened, rules match events by pattern, and matching events go to targets (Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, APIs, other buses). Producers don't know consumers, so systems can be loosely coupled and extended without changing the sender.

first_principles.problem: The order service calls billing, shipping and email directly, and adding a new consumer means redeploying it.
truths: New consumers should subscribe without producer changes.

analogy.title: The body's nervous system
analogy.story: Sensors send signals; the brain routes them to whichever muscles need to react.
analogy.breaks: Nerves are hard-wired; EventBridge routes are reconfigured by adding rules.

example.title: Decoupled order flow
flow: New loyalty service adds its own rule

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No change to the order service.

check.q: How does EventBridge decouple producers from consumers?
check.a: Producers publish to a bus without knowing who consumes; rules route events to targets independently.

event-buses-default-custom-and-partner.core: The default bus receives AWS service events (EC2 state changes, S3 notifications, CloudTrail API calls). Custom buses carry your application's events, scoped by domain or team with their own resource policies. Partner buses receive events from SaaS providers (Zendesk, Datadog, Auth0). Buses can forward events across accounts and regions.

first_principles.problem: All teams publish to the default bus, making permissions and rule management chaotic.
truths: Central buses aggregate events from many accounts.
derivation: **Custom bus per domain** for app events.

analogy.title: Separate radio channels
analogy.story: Emergency services, airport and taxis each use their own channel.
analogy.breaks: Radio channels broadcast to anyone listening; buses only deliver to matching rules.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Orders domain isolated with clear publish rights.

code.text:
aws events create-event-bus --name orders
aws events put-permission --event-bus-name orders --action events:PutEvents \
  --principal 111122223333 --statement-id allow-orders-account

check.q: Where do AWS service events like EC2 state changes arrive?

events-the-json-payload.core: Every event has an envelope (version, id, source, detail-type, account, time, region, resources) and a detail object holding the domain payload, up to 256 KB. Good events are past-tense facts with stable fields, include enough context for consumers, and are versioned.

first_principles.problem: Events carry only an ID, so every consumer calls back to the producer and overloads it.
derivation: Keep under **256 KB** (claim-check large data in S3).

analogy.title: A standard shipping label plus the parcel contents
analogy.story: The label lets sorters route it; the contents serve the recipient.
analogy.breaks: Parcels are opened once; events are read by many consumers who all depend on its shape.

check.q: What's the maximum EventBridge event size?

rules-the-routing-logic.core: Rules match events with JSON patterns on any field: exact values, prefix/suffix, numeric ranges, anything-but, exists and wildcard. Each rule can route to up to five targets and can transform input. Schedule-based rules (and EventBridge Scheduler) trigger targets on cron/rate expressions.

first_principles.problem: A billing Lambda receives every order event and filters in code, wasting invocations.
truths: Filtering at the bus is cheaper than in code.
Patterns match structure, not just strings.

analogy.title: Email filters
analogy.story: 'If from the bank and subject contains invoice, move to Finance folder.'
analogy.breaks: Email filters act on one inbox; rules deliver one event to many targets at once.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fraud check runs only on big orders.

check.q: Why filter with rule patterns instead of in the target?
check.a: It avoids invoking targets for irrelevant events, cutting cost and complexity.

targets-and-delivery-guarantees.core: EventBridge delivers at least once to targets, retrying with backoff for up to 24 hours (configurable retry count and max event age). Failed events can go to a dead-letter SQS queue. Order isn't guaranteed and duplicates can happen, so consumers must be idempotent and must not rely on ordering.

first_principles.problem: A target outage silently drops events, and duplicates double-charge customers.

analogy.title: A courier who keeps redelivering until someone signs
analogy.story: You might get the parcel twice if the first signature was lost.
analogy.breaks: Couriers deliver in sequence; events can arrive out of order.

check.a: No; events may arrive out of order and more than once.

schema-registry-the-contract-between-tea.core: The EventBridge Schema Registry stores event schemas (OpenAPI/JSONSchema), can discover them automatically from bus traffic, and generates code bindings. Schemas act as contracts between producing and consuming teams, enabling validation, documentation and safe evolution through versions.

first_principles.problem: A producer renames a field and three consumer teams break in production.
derivation: Communicate **breaking changes** with a new detail-type or version.

analogy.title: A published API specification
analogy.story: Teams build against the documented contract, not guesswork.
analogy.breaks: API specs are often enforced by gateways; EventBridge doesn't reject non-conforming events by default.

steps.label: Rule
steps.detail: Renames and removals = new major version.

check.q: What kind of schema change is safe for existing consumers?
check.a: Adding optional fields; renaming or removing fields is breaking.

eventbridge-pipes-point-to-point-enrichm.core: EventBridge Pipes connect one source (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, Kafka, MQ) to one target with optional filtering, enrichment (Lambda, Step Functions, API Gateway, API destinations) and transformation, replacing glue Lambda functions with managed configuration.

first_principles.problem: Dozens of tiny Lambdas exist only to read a stream, call an API for extra data and forward results.

analogy.title: A plumbing pipe with a filter and a water softener built in
analogy.story: Water flows from one tank to another, cleaned along the way.
analogy.breaks: Pipes carry water continuously; EventBridge Pipes process records in batches.

check.q: How do Pipes differ from bus rules?
check.a: Pipes connect one source to one target point-to-point with enrichment; rules fan out events from a bus to many targets.

architectural-patterns-and-production-co.core: Production event-driven systems need: a clear bus topology (per-domain buses, central hub), idempotent consumers, DLQs and alarms, archive and replay for recovery, quotas awareness (PutEvents TPS, invocation rates), observability (event IDs in logs, tracing), and governance over schemas and ownership.

first_principles.problem: An event-driven system becomes an untraceable web where nobody knows which consumer failed.

analogy.title: Air traffic management for messages
analogy.story: Flight plans, radar, holding patterns and incident replay keep busy skies safe.
analogy.breaks: Planes are tracked individually by default; events need explicit correlation to trace.

example.title: Recovering from a consumer bug
flow: Bug in loyalty consumer for 3 hours
Replay archive for that window to loyalty rule

check.q: What makes replaying archived events safe?
check.a: Idempotent consumers, so reprocessed events don't cause duplicate side effects.
